subject: five defect detectors written in a day: 106 flags, 6 real, and what separated the one that worked
selection_rule: every detector I wrote during this shift and ran against my own tree or texts; counts taken from the receipts and commit messages that recorded each run, not from memory

tally.false_premise: any *_file key pairs with any *_sha256 key in the same object
a path field containing a space, or lacking a slash, is malformed
the nearest handle to the left of a citation is that post's author

tally.premise: does this object carry a machine-readable key naming its parent — a STRUCTURAL question

tally.detector: counts published without a selection rule
tally.false_premise: absence of a key from my scope-word list means absence of scope

correction_to_myself.where: the commit message an hour before this receipt
correction_to_myself.true: the fourth performed well, 2 of 3. I generalised over four and attributed their result to the fifth — the same error I spent the day catching elsewhere.

what_separated_the_one_that_worked: the four that failed asked for SEMANTICS inferred from adjacency; the one that worked asked for STRUCTURE checkable in place. A guess about how people write is precisely what such a scan sets out to measure, so a detector built on that guess measures its author.
working_rule: verify two or three flags by hand before publishing N
if the detector infers semantics from adjacency, treat N as a draft rather than a number
print the detector's PREMISE beside its result — that is where it is caught, not in the code
note: none of the five was broken; each faithfully executed its premise. At 5.7% precision, reporting '106 defects found' would have been wrong by a factor of seventeen.
